title: The First Key to Connecting Well with All Students is to Like Them -takes-work/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. opens with a hallway conversation with a struggling ninth grader, Kandyce, to show what genuine teacher-student connection looks like. He then asks how teachers can build education-focused relationships with students who seem impossibly behind or unmotivated, and answers that the only route is to actually like them. Stuart admits he has to work at this, describing a set of inner practices: imagining himself in the student's shoes, hunting for redeeming qualities, praying for the student, and observing them like a researcher. He argues that relationships are built one moment of real connection at a time and that there is no shortcut around this inner work. He closes by noting a side benefit: the practice makes him less easily offended and less self-focused, which keeps him engaged in teaching.
points: Genuine liking, not technique, is the foundation of relationships with the hardest-to-reach students, because students can sense whether care is real.
Stuart models talking about grades without shame, framing GPA as a number to improve one point at a time.
He lists concrete inner exercises, such as seeking redeeming qualities and taking researcher-style notes, for when liking a student does not come naturally.
The work of liking students also shapes the teacher's character, reducing defensiveness and self-focus.
quotes: But here’s the question: how do we build strong, education-focused relationships with students like Kandyce, who seem impossibly behind, impossibly under-motivated? How do we communicate with them about school — a topic that often equals threat in their hearts — and at the same time communicate genuine care?

Listen, I know school is a struggle for you. So we get that GPA better just one point at a time, okay? And since I’m your teacher, I am going to talk to you about it sometimes, because I care about you.
It’s that word “genuine” that is both the bugger and the solution. The only way is to actually like our students.

I admit that I have to work hard to like some of my students. Many of them say or do things that can, if I’m sloppy with the inner work, hurt my feelings or cause resentment or make me want to write them off.

I look for redeeming qualities in them: in their smiles, their senses of humor, their odd mannerisms, their impromptu confessions. I go through spiritual exercises of praying for them and asking God to help me like them. I make notes about them on the clipboard, imagining myself as a researcher studying a world that has never been studied before.

I have so many points in each week where an interaction with a student tempts me toward not liking them. But I’ve learned that the internal work described in the above paragraph keeps me in range of the most powerful force for building good relationships with human beings: actually liking them. These relationships are built one moment of genuine connection at a time.
One last thing: This work has a blessed side effect, too. In my own life, I become less easily offended, less self-focused, less “all about me.
